newsitem.title: SPAIN: INSTANT VIEW - Spanish Q4, 1996 GDP.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Spanish Q4, 1996 GDP.

text.p: Following is a selection of economists' reactions to Spanish fourth-quarter and 1996 gross domestic product data.
In the fourth quarter, GDP rose 2.6 percent year on year after 2.2 percent in the third quarter. In 1996, GDP rose 2.2 percent versus 2.8 percent in 1995.
The government had forecast 1996 GDP growth of 2.3 percent.
ALFREDO URRUTIA, ECONOMIST AT SOCIETE GENERALE IN MADRID
"The data are good, a little bit better than we expected...as it's a figure that was anticipated it's unlikely to move the market."
CARMEN HERNANSANZ, ECONOMIST AT MERRILL LYNCH, MADRID.

"GDP was in line with forecasts. In principle, it seems we've got over the transitory slump in the last phase of 1995 and the first part of 1996. As far as components are concerned, they're not inflationary, given that private consumption is still accelerating, but moderately. The weaker tone of fixed capital formation is explained by the fall in construction. GDP components are not going to stop the Bank of Spain continuing to cut rates."
HENRIK LUMHOLDT, ECONOMIST AT BANK OF AMERICA, MADRID

"All the components were within our expectations, except exports. We had forecast 2.2 percent (for the quarter). The rise in exports and moderation in imports explains 0.2 percentage points of difference. The rest of the difference stems from a revision (in) 1995 numbers. That is the third revision of 1995 numbers. It is almost impossible to make a forecast.

"For the whole of 1996, we had expected 2.1 percent...Looking ahead, you can expect no increase in exports. Private consumption will remain at current growth rates. Capital goods could well lose some of their buoyancy, but construction can hardly remain as depressed as it has been.
"Overall, we see 2.4 percent for 1997. We will improve, but it's still a far shot from the government's 3.0-percent forecast."
COLIN WARREN, ECONOMIST AT TOKAI BANK LONDON
"This figure is slightly stronger than the Bank of Spain said, but private consumption growth remains low.
"Overall, the data is good. This figure doesn't show an economy on the verge of recession as is the case in Italy. So, it is not putting pressure on the Bank of Spain to cut rates short term.
"A significant part of growth is due to external demand, while the domestic component remains subdued.

"There are lot of factors keeping consumption low, and I think this is one of the reasons keeping the government away from a sweeping reform of the labour market. Such a thing would risk giving consumer confidence a knock again.
"We had a good rise in 1996 unemployment, which under normal circumstances, should give a higher boost to consumer confidence.
"But there is also the prospect of a possible fiscal squeeze during this year.
"With fairly low growth, a weak peseta and a very tough target for inflation in 1998, I don't think the Bank of Spain should feel any urgency to cut rates."
VALENTIN FERNANDEZ, ECONOMIST AT CREDIT LYONNAIS

"The number was slightly above expectations, but only slightly. Private consumption rose a tenth in comparison with the third quarter, which represents a moderate recovery with no inflation threat. The improvement in GDP was helped by the export sector where there was a real rate of 12.1 percent, which hasn't been so high for long. This sector is giving key signs of strength that points to the competitiveness of the Spanish economy...
"Investment continues in a latent state while construction can't get going, probably because of contraction in the public sector."
But Fernandez said these numbers do not put future interest rate cuts from the Bank of Spain at risk.
